passage.title: The Changing Role of Workplace Mentors

paragraphs.text: Many companies once treated mentoring as an informal activity that depended on a generous and experienced colleague. Today, however, some organizations are designing mentoring programs deliberately. They pair newer employees with more experienced workers, often from different departments. The purpose is not simply to teach technical procedures. Mentors may also explain unwritten workplace expectations, such as how decisions are made, how meetings are conducted, and when it is appropriate to ask for assistance.

This arrangement can benefit both sides. New employees usually gain confidence because they have someone to consult before a small problem becomes a serious one. They may also understand the organization more quickly than they would through written instructions alone. Experienced employees, meanwhile, often discover that explaining familiar tasks forces them to examine their own habits. In addition, conversations with younger colleagues can introduce them to new software, communication styles, or customer expectations.

Nevertheless, a mentoring program does not automatically produce these results. A mentor who sees the role as another administrative duty may offer only hurried advice. Similarly, a new employee who expects the mentor to solve every difficulty may fail to develop independence. For this reason, effective programs establish clear boundaries: mentors provide guidance and perspective, but they do not make decisions on behalf of their partners. Regular meetings are useful, yet the relationship also needs enough flexibility to respond to genuine concerns.

The strongest programs therefore measure success in broader ways than counting meetings. Managers may look at whether new employees become comfortable seeking information, cooperating across departments, and taking responsibility for their work. These outcomes take time and cannot be attributed entirely to mentoring, since training and personal effort also matter. Even so, a well-supported mentoring relationship can make the workplace easier to understand while encouraging experienced employees to remain active learners.

passage.title: Rethinking Homework in the Digital Classroom

paragraphs.text: As digital tools become common in schools, teachers are reconsidering the role of homework. Online platforms can make assignments easier to distribute and allow students to receive quick feedback. They can also help teachers notice which questions cause difficulty. However, technology does not automatically make homework more useful. An activity placed online may still be repetitive, confusing, or unrelated to what students need to learn.

Some teachers now use short online tasks before a lesson. Students may watch a brief explanation, answer a few questions, or collect an example from daily life. The teacher then uses their responses to adjust the lesson. This approach can be effective because it gives students a reason to prepare and gives teachers information in advance. Nevertheless, it depends on reliable internet access and on students understanding what they are expected to do.

Other educators prefer assignments that require students to work away from a screen. A student might interview a family member about a local tradition, measure objects at home, or explain a scientific idea in a notebook. Such tasks can connect school subjects with ordinary experience. They are not necessarily easier to assess, however, since students may receive different kinds of help at home. For this reason, teachers often combine these activities with a short in-class discussion.

The most promising approach is therefore not to choose between digital and traditional homework. Instead, teachers can select the format according to the learning goal. An online quiz may suit factual review, while a conversation or practical task may better develop communication and observation. Good homework is not defined by its appearance but by whether it helps students think, gives teachers useful information, and remains manageable for learners with different circumstances.

paragraphs.text: For much of the twentieth century, wetlands inside or near cities were treated as useless land. They were drained for roads, factories, and housing, partly because planners associated standing water with disease and unpleasant smells. Today, however, many cities are reconsidering this approach. Urban wetlands can absorb rainwater, support wildlife, reduce heat, and provide residents with places to walk and observe nature. Their value is not simply decorative: when heavy rain falls, the plants and soft soil of a wetland can temporarily hold water that might otherwise flood streets and buildings.

The flood-control function of a wetland depends on its condition. A healthy wetland contains layers of plants, open water, and waterlogged soil, each slowing the movement of water in a different way. If people cover too much of the area with concrete, or if polluted water enters it, this system becomes less effective. Restoration therefore involves more than removing rubbish. Engineers may reshape channels, reconnect a wetland to a river, and create shallow areas where native plants can grow. These changes are usually designed to work with natural processes rather than replace them.

Wetlands also influence the temperature of urban neighborhoods. Water releases heat slowly, while vegetation provides shade and cools the air through evaporation. As a result, a restored wetland may make nearby streets more comfortable during a heat wave. This benefit is not distributed equally, however. A wetland surrounded by busy roads may offer little relief to residents who cannot safely reach it. For that reason, some projects include footpaths, shaded entrances, and public transport links. Access is considered part of environmental planning, not an optional extra.

Restoration can bring difficulties as well as benefits. New ponds may attract insects, and poorly maintained areas can become clogged with invasive plants. Nearby residents may also worry that a project will increase mosquitoes or reduce land available for construction. These concerns should not simply be dismissed. Regular monitoring, careful water circulation, and clear information can reduce some risks, while early consultation can reveal practical problems before construction begins. In this way, community involvement improves not only public support but also the design itself.

The success of an urban wetland should therefore be judged over time and by several measures. Scientists may record water levels, plant diversity, and the number of animal species, while local authorities may examine flood damage and maintenance costs. Residents’ experiences matter too: a wetland that performs well ecologically but feels unsafe or inaccessible will not serve the whole community. Urban wetland restoration is consequently neither a quick engineering fix nor a purely recreational project. It is a long-term attempt to connect natural processes with the practical needs of city life.

passage.title: How Small Changes Improve a Workday

paragraphs.text: Many people think a better workday begins with a louder alarm or a stronger cup of coffee, but small habits often matter more than dramatic changes. In several offices, workers who start by planning the first 20 minutes of the day usually feel less rushed. They are not doing extra work; instead, they are deciding what deserves attention first. This simple habit can reduce the time spent switching between emails, messages, and unfinished tasks. When people know the first step, the rest of the morning may feel more manageable.

Breaks also shape how people perform. A short pause away from the screen can help a person notice mistakes that were easy to miss a few minutes earlier. Some employees avoid breaks because they worry about seeming unproductive, yet constant concentration is not always efficient. After a brief walk, stretch, or quiet moment, the mind often returns to the task with more focus. The benefit is not that the break itself solves the job, but that it gives the brain a chance to recover from fatigue.

Workplaces that improve communication often do so in practical ways. For example, teams may agree on one place to share updates, rather than sending the same information in several chat groups. This does not make communication faster only because there are fewer messages; it also reduces confusion about which version is final. When instructions are clear, workers spend less time checking details and more time completing tasks correctly. In this way, order in communication can support both speed and accuracy.

These changes are usually modest, but they can have a noticeable effect over a week. A worker who plans the morning, takes a short break, and receives clearer messages may still face busy days and unexpected problems. However, the day may end with less stress and fewer unfinished tasks. The lesson is not that simple habits remove all pressure from work. Rather, they make demanding schedules easier to handle by preventing small problems from growing into bigger ones.

reading_items.notes: The passage consistently frames the author as favoring balance and moderate change.
Positive but conditional view is directly supported by paragraph 2.
Paragraph 3 explicitly rejects judging technology by novelty alone.
Paragraph 4 presents homework as context-dependent rather than fixed-rule.
‘Careful attitude’ is described as leading to practical decisions, so ‘practical’ is the best characterization.

paragraphs.text: In many schools, teachers are asked to do more than explain lessons. They are expected to help students solve problems, work in groups, and use digital tools while still mastering the basics of reading, writing, and mathematics. This change has led to lively debate. Some people think classrooms should look almost the same as they did twenty years ago. Others believe schools must change quickly to match the world outside. In practice, most educators now search for a middle path rather than a dramatic answer.

One popular idea is project-based learning, where students spend time investigating a question and creating something to share with the class. Supporters say it keeps learners interested because it connects schoolwork to real life. Critics worry that projects can become noisy and unfocused if they are not carefully planned. The strongest programs seem to combine both views: they give students freedom, but they also provide clear steps and regular feedback. In that sense, the method is less a replacement for teaching than a different way of organizing it.

Technology has created a similar mix of hope and caution. Digital exercises can give quick practice and immediate results, which helps teachers notice where students are struggling. However, a tablet does not automatically improve learning just because it is modern. If students click through activities without thinking, the device becomes a distraction instead of a tool. For that reason, many schools are learning to judge technology by how well it supports a lesson, not by how new it appears.

Even homework, often treated as a simple good-or-bad issue, is usually more complicated. Too much homework can leave students tired and unhappy, yet no homework at all may make it harder to build study habits. The most convincing approach is not to choose one extreme but to ask what kind of task fits the age of the learners and the goal of the lesson. That careful attitude may sound modest, but it often leads to more practical decisions than bold slogans do.

questions.explanation_vi: Tác giả không phản đối công nghệ, nhưng cũng không tin rằng mọi thiết bị hiện đại đều tốt. Ông ủng hộ công nghệ khi nó phục vụ bài học một cách hiệu quả.

A.explanation_vi: Sai vì tác giả cảnh báo rằng thiết bị có thể trở thành sự xao nhãng nếu học sinh dùng máy móc.

B.explanation_vi: Sai vì tác giả thừa nhận công nghệ có thể giúp luyện tập nhanh và cho kết quả ngay.

C.explanation_vi: Sai vì bài đọc không nói công nghệ nên thay thế hầu hết hoạt động trên lớp.

D.explanation_vi: Đúng vì tác giả đánh giá công nghệ theo tác dụng thực sự với việc học, chứ không theo sự mới mẻ của nó.

evidence.quote: many schools are learning to judge technology by how well it supports a lesson, not by how new it appears.

questions.question_text: What does the author think about homework?

options.A: He believes homework is always harmful to students.
options.B: He thinks homework is simple and should be the same for all learners.
options.C: He feels homework should never be used in modern education.
options.D: He sees it as a matter that needs careful judgment rather than a fixed rule.

questions.explanation_vi: Tác giả không xem bài tập về nhà là hoàn toàn tốt hay hoàn toàn xấu. Ông nhấn mạnh phải cân nhắc độ tuổi và mục tiêu bài học, tức là cần đánh giá linh hoạt.

A.explanation_vi: Sai vì bài đọc chỉ nói quá nhiều bài tập có thể làm học sinh mệt, không phải luôn luôn có hại.

B.explanation_vi: Sai vì tác giả cho rằng vấn đề này phức tạp, không thể áp dụng một công thức giống nhau cho mọi người.

C.explanation_vi: Sai vì bài đọc không phản đối hoàn toàn homework; ngược lại, còn thừa nhận nó có thể giúp xây dựng thói quen học tập.

D.explanation_vi: Đúng vì tác giả khuyến nghị xem xét loại bài tập phù hợp thay vì áp dụng một quy tắc cứng nhắc.

evidence.quote: The most convincing approach is not to choose one extreme but to ask what kind of task fits the age of the learners and the goal of the lesson.

questions.question_text: How would the author most likely describe the “careful attitude” mentioned in the last paragraph?

options.A: As a weak attitude that avoids making any decisions
options.B: As a practical attitude that aims for useful decisions
options.C: As an old-fashioned attitude that rejects all innovation
options.D: As a confusing attitude that makes lessons harder to plan

questions.explanation_vi: Ở cuối bài, tác giả nói thái độ thận trọng tuy nghe có vẻ khiêm tốn nhưng thường dẫn đến quyết định thực tế hơn các khẩu hiệu lớn. Vì thế, đó là thái độ thực dụng và hữu ích.

A.explanation_vi: Sai vì tác giả không cho rằng thận trọng là né tránh quyết định; ngược lại, nó giúp chọn giải pháp tốt hơn.

B.explanation_vi: Đúng vì bài đọc trực tiếp nói thái độ này thường dẫn đến những quyết định thực tế hơn.

C.explanation_vi: Sai vì tác giả không xem sự thận trọng là chống đổi mới; ông nhấn mạnh cân bằng và phù hợp.

D.explanation_vi: Sai vì đoạn cuối đánh giá thái độ này là hữu ích, không phải gây rối cho việc lập kế hoạch.

evidence.quote: That careful attitude may sound modest, but it often leads to more practical decisions than bold slogans do.
